subject: maths
title: Circle properties: angles and chords
summary: The circle theorems for angles (centre, same segment, semicircle, cyclic quadrilaterals) and chords, used with reasons and Pythagoras.
body:
A circle looks simple, but the angles and chords inside it follow a set of surprisingly neat rules. Designers of arches, wheels, gears and stadiums use them, and they let you find unknown angles in a circle without a protractor.

## Learning objective

By the end of this lesson you can name the parts of a circle and use the circle theorems for angles (centre, same segment, semicircle, cyclic quadrilateral) and chords (perpendicular from the centre bisects a chord) to find unknown angles and lengths, giving reasons.

## Before you start

You need "Angle properties review (Year 9)", "Pythagoras' theorem review (Year 9)" and "Geometric proofs and congruence" from this chapter — especially isosceles triangles.

Warm-up:
1. An isosceles triangle has an apex angle of 40°. Find each base angle.
2. Find √(13² − 5²).

Answers: 1. (180° − 40°) ÷ 2 = 70°  2. √(169 − 25) = √144 = 12

## Think of it like this

### Watching a stage from a curved balcony

Imagine a stage that sits on the edge of a circular theatre, with seats all round the curved wall. Every seat on the far side of the theatre sees the stage at exactly the same angle — sitting further along the curve doesn't change it. A director standing at the very centre sees the stage at twice that angle.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* real theatres aren't perfect circles, and a seat on the same side as the stage (the other segment) sees it at a different angle — the two angles add to 180°.

## Key ideas

### Parts of a circle

A **chord** is a segment joining two points on the circle; a **diameter** is a chord through the centre O. An **arc** is part of the circumference. A chord splits the circle into two **segments** (minor and major). An angle **subtended** by an arc at a point is the angle formed by joining the arc's ends to that point. Every radius is the same length, so triangles made with two radii are **isosceles**.

### Angle at the centre

![Points A, B and C on a circle with centre O. Angle ACB is θ and angle AOB is 2θ](diagrams/y10/maths/circle-properties-angles-and-chords-centre.svg)

The angle at the centre is **twice** the angle at the circumference standing on the same arc: ∠AOB = 2 × ∠ACB.

*Why:* join C to O and extend. OA = OC = OB (radii), so each of the two small triangles is isosceles. Each outside angle at O equals the sum of the two equal base angles, so it is double the angle at C. Adding the two parts gives 2θ.

### Angles in the same segment, and the semicircle

Angles at the circumference standing on the same arc (in the same segment) are **equal**, because each is half the same angle at the centre.

![AB is a diameter and C is a point on the circle; angle ACB is a right angle](diagrams/y10/maths/circle-properties-angles-and-chords-semi.svg)

If the arc is a semicircle (AB is a diameter), the angle at the centre is a straight angle, 180°, so the **angle in a semicircle is 90°**.

### Cyclic quadrilaterals

![Cyclic quadrilateral ABCD with angle A marked a and angle C marked 180° − a](diagrams/y10/maths/circle-properties-angles-and-chords-cyclic.svg)

A **cyclic quadrilateral** has all four vertices on a circle. Its **opposite angles add to 180°** (they are supplementary), because together they stand on the whole circle: half of 360° is 180°.

### Chords

![A chord AB with the perpendicular from the centre O meeting it at M, so AM = MB](diagrams/y10/maths/circle-properties-angles-and-chords-chord.svg)

The perpendicular from the centre to a chord **bisects** the chord (cuts it in half). Triangles OMA and OMB are congruent (RHS: right angle, OA = OB, OM common), so AM = MB. This gives a right-angled triangle OMA you can use with Pythagoras. Equal chords are the same distance from the centre.

## Worked examples

### Example 1

![Points A, B and C on a circle with centre O; angle AOB = 130° and angle ACB = x](diagrams/y10/maths/circle-properties-angles-and-chords-ex1.svg)

Find x.

Step 1: ∠AOB and ∠ACB both stand on arc AB — check the arc first.
Step 2: angle at the centre = 2 × angle at the circumference, so x = 130° ÷ 2.
Step 3: x = 65°.

### Example 2

AB is a diameter and C is on the circle. ∠CAB = 34°. Find ∠ABC.

Step 1: ∠ACB = 90° — angle in a semicircle.
Step 2: ∠ABC = 180° − 90° − 34° — angle sum of triangle ABC.
Step 3: ∠ABC = 56°.

### Example 3

![Cyclic quadrilateral ABCD with angle A = (3x + 10)° and angle C = (2x − 5)°](diagrams/y10/maths/circle-properties-angles-and-chords-ex3.svg)

ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral with ∠A = (3x + 10)° and ∠C = (2x − 5)°. Find x and ∠A.

Step 1: A and C are opposite, so (3x + 10) + (2x − 5) = 180 — opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral.
Step 2: 5x + 5 = 180, so 5x = 175 and x = 35.
Step 3: ∠A = 3 × 35 + 10 = 115°.

Check: ∠C = 2 × 35 − 5 = 65° and 115° + 65° = 180° ✓

### Example 4

![A chord AB of length 16 cm in a circle of radius 10 cm, with the perpendicular distance d from O to the chord](diagrams/y10/maths/circle-properties-angles-and-chords-ex4.svg)

A chord 16 cm long is in a circle of radius 10 cm. How far is it from the centre?

Step 1: the perpendicular from O bisects the chord, so AM = 16 ÷ 2 = 8 cm.
Step 2: in right-angled triangle OMA the hypotenuse is the radius OA = 10 cm.
Step 3: d² = 10² − 8² = 100 − 64 = 36, so d = 6 cm.

## Common mistakes

- **Doubling the wrong way.** The centre angle is the BIG one. Fix: centre = 2 × circumference, so circumference = centre ÷ 2.
- **Using different arcs.** The rules only work when both angles stand on the same arc. Fix: trace the two arms of each angle to the circle and check they land on the same two points.
- **Adding to 360° instead of 180°.** In a cyclic quadrilateral only *opposite* angles add to 180°. Fix: pair A with C, and B with D.
- **Using the whole chord in Pythagoras.** Fix: halve the chord first; the radius is always the hypotenuse.
- **Forgetting isosceles triangles.** Two radii make an isosceles triangle. Fix: mark every radius as equal.

## Tips to remember

- **"Centre is double."** The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the edge on the same arc.
- **"Bow-tie angles match."** (A made-up memory trick.) Angles in the same segment form a bow-tie shape with equal angles at the ends.
- **"Diameter → right angle."** Spot a diameter? Look for a 90° angle at the circumference.
- **"Opposite friends add to 180."** Opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary.
- **"Halve the chord, radius on top."** For chords: half-chord, distance and radius make a right-angled triangle with the radius as hypotenuse.

## Key terms

- **Chord** — a segment joining two points on a circle.
- **Arc** — part of the circumference.
- **Segment** — the region between a chord and an arc.
- **Subtended angle** — the angle formed at a point by lines from the ends of an arc or chord.
- **Cyclic quadrilateral** — a quadrilateral with all four vertices on a circle.
- **Bisect** — cut into two equal parts.

## Summary

- Angle at the centre = 2 × angle at the circumference on the same arc.
- Angles in the same segment are equal; the angle in a semicircle is 90°.
- Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add to 180°.
- The perpendicular from the centre bisects a chord; use Pythagoras with the radius as hypotenuse.
- Radii are equal, so look for isosceles triangles.

questions.prompt: O is the centre of the circle. Find x.
questions.explanation: Both angles stand on arc AB, so x = 110° ÷ 2 = 55°. Doubling (220°) gets the rule the wrong way around.
steps: ∠AOB and x both stand on arc AB.
Angle at the centre = 2 × angle at the circumference.

mistakes.A: Step 2: the angle at the circumference is not equal to the angle at the centre — it is half of it.
mistakes.C: Step 2: you doubled. The angle at the CENTRE is the double one, so halve 110°.
mistakes.D: Step 1: 180° − 110° is for angles on a line or in a cyclic quadrilateral. Here both angles stand on arc AB, so halve.

questions.diagram_alt: A circle with centre O. Points A and B are on the lower part of the circle and C at the top. Angle AOB is 110° and angle ACB is x.

questions.prompt: AB is a diameter of the circle and ∠CAB = 25°. Find x, the size of ∠ABC.
questions.explanation: AB is a diameter, so ∠ACB = 90°. Then x = 180° − 90° − 25° = 65°. Forgetting the right angle gives 155°.
steps: AB is a diameter, so ∠ACB = 90° (angle in a semicircle).
Angles in triangle ABC add to 180°.

mistakes.A: Step 2: ∠ABC is not equal to ∠CAB. Use the triangle angle sum with the right angle at C.
mistakes.B: Step 1: the 90° angle is at C (angle in a semicircle), not at B.
mistakes.C: Step 2: you subtracted only 25° from 180°. The triangle also has the 90° angle at C.

questions.diagram_alt: A circle with diameter AB drawn horizontally and a point C on the upper right of the circle. Angle CAB is 25° and angle ABC is x.

questions.explanation: ∠ACB and ∠ADB both stand on arc AB from the same side, so they are equal: x = 48°. Doubling is only for an angle at the centre.
steps: C and D are both on the circle, on the same side of chord AB.
Angles in the same segment (on the same arc) are equal.

mistakes.B: Step 2: you doubled. Both angles are at the circumference, so they are equal — no doubling.
mistakes.C: Step 2: you halved. Both angles are at the circumference on the same arc, so they are equal.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 180° − 48° is for opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral. C and D are in the same segment.

questions.diagram_alt: A circle with chord AB near the bottom. Points C and D are on the upper part of the circle; both are joined to A and B. Angle ADB is 48° and angle ACB is x.

questions.prompt: ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral with ∠A = 82°. Find x, the size of ∠C.
questions.explanation: A and C are opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral, so x = 180° − 82° = 98°. They are not equal (82°).
steps: All four vertices are on the circle, so ABCD is cyclic.
A and C are opposite, so ∠A + ∠C = 180°.

mistakes.A: Step 2: opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are not equal — they add to 180°.
mistakes.B: Step 2: there is no centre angle here. Opposite angles add to 180°, so subtract.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 360° is the angle sum of all four angles. Only the opposite pair A and C adds to 180°.

questions.diagram_alt: A cyclic quadrilateral ABCD drawn inside a circle. Angle A is 82° and the opposite angle C is x.

questions.prompt: A chord AB is 5 cm from the centre O of a circle with radius 13 cm. Find x, the length of the chord.
questions.explanation: AM² = 13² − 5² = 144, so AM = 12 cm, and the chord is 2 × 12 = 24 cm. 12 cm is only half of it.
steps: The perpendicular OM bisects AB, and OA = 13 cm is the hypotenuse of triangle OMA.

mistakes.B: Step 3: 12 cm is AM, only half the chord. The perpendicular bisects AB, so double it.
mistakes.C: Step 2: the radius is the hypotenuse, so subtract the squares: 13² − 5².
mistakes.D: Step 2: you subtracted the lengths 13 − 5. Square them first.

questions.diagram_alt: A circle with centre O. Chord AB has midpoint M; OM is 5 cm and meets AB at a right angle. Radius OA is 13 cm and the chord AB is marked x.

questions.prompt: O is the centre and ∠ACB = 38°. Find x, the size of ∠OAB.
questions.explanation: ∠AOB = 2 × 38° = 76°. OA = OB (radii), so x = (180° − 76°) ÷ 2 = 52°. Using 38° as the apex gives 71°.
steps: ∠AOB = 2 × ∠ACB = 2 × 38° = 76° (angle at the centre).
OA = OB (radii), so triangle OAB is isosceles with equal base angles.

mistakes.A: Step 1 only: 76° is ∠AOB. Now use isosceles triangle OAB to find the base angle.
mistakes.B: Step 1: ∠OAB is not equal to ∠ACB. First double 38° to get ∠AOB.
mistakes.C: Step 2: you used 38° as the angle at O. The angle at O is double: 76°.

questions.diagram_alt: A circle with centre O, point C at the top, and A and B on the lower part. C is joined to A and B, O is joined to A and B, and A is joined to B. Angle ACB is 38° and angle OAB is x.

questions.prompt: ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral with ∠B = (4x − 6)° and ∠D = (2x + 18)°. Find the size of ∠B.
questions.explanation: Opposite angles add to 180°: 6x + 12 = 180, so x = 28 and ∠B = 4 × 28 − 6 = 106°. Setting them equal gives 42°.
steps: B and D are opposite, so (4x − 6) + (2x + 18) = 180.

mistakes.A: Step 3: x = 28 is not the angle. Substitute it into 4x − 6.
mistakes.B: Step 3: 74° is ∠D. Substitute x into the expression for ∠B instead.
mistakes.D: Step 1: B and D are not equal — opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add to 180°.

questions.diagram_alt: A cyclic quadrilateral ABCD inside a circle, with angle B labelled (4x − 6)° and the opposite angle D labelled (2x + 18)°.

questions.prompt: A chord 10 cm long is drawn in a circle of radius 7 cm. Find d, its distance from the centre, correct to 1 decimal place. (Calculator allowed.)
questions.explanation: Half the chord is 5 cm, so d² = 7² − 5² = 24 and d = √24 ≈ 4.9 cm. Adding the squares gives 8.6 cm, which is longer than the radius — impossible.
steps: The perpendicular from O bisects the chord: half-chord = 10 ÷ 2 = 5 cm.
The radius 7 cm is the hypotenuse of the right-angled triangle.

mistakes.A: Step 3: the radius is the hypotenuse, so subtract: 7² − 5², don't add.
mistakes.C: Step 3: you subtracted the lengths 7 − 5. Square them first, then take the square root.
mistakes.D: Step 1: halve the chord first. You used the whole 10 cm chord with the 7 cm radius: √(10² − 7²).

questions.diagram_alt: A circle with centre O and radius OA of 7 cm. Chord AB is 10 cm long. A dashed perpendicular d from O meets the chord at its midpoint M.

questions.prompt: AB is a diameter and ∠CAB = 28°. D is another point on the circle, as shown. Find x, the size of ∠ADC.
questions.explanation: ∠ACB = 90° (semicircle), so ∠ABC = 180° − 90° − 28° = 62°. ∠ADC and ∠ABC stand on the same arc AC, so x = 62°. Using 180° − 62° = 118° would be for opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral.
steps: ∠ACB = 90° (angle in a semicircle).
∠ABC = 180° − 90° − 28° = 62° (angle sum of triangle ABC).
∠ADC and ∠ABC stand on arc AC in the same segment, so x = 62°.

mistakes.A: Step 3: ∠ADC stands on arc AC, so it equals ∠ABC — not ∠CAB.
mistakes.B: Step 1: the right angle is ∠ACB (in the semicircle on AB). ∠ADC is not on a diameter.
mistakes.C: Step 3: D and B are on the same side of chord AC, so the angles are equal, not supplementary.

questions.diagram_alt: A circle with horizontal diameter AB. C is on the upper right of the circle and D on the lower right. Segments AC, CB, AD and DC are drawn. Angle CAB is 28° and angle ADC is x.

questions.prompt: O is the centre. ∠ABC = 115°, where B is on the minor arc AC. Find x, the size of the non-reflex angle AOC.
questions.explanation: ∠ABC stands on the major arc AC, so the reflex ∠AOC = 2 × 115° = 230° and x = 360° − 230° = 130°. 230° is the reflex angle, not x.
steps: ∠ABC = 115° stands on the major arc AC (the arc not containing B).
The reflex angle AOC on that arc = 2 × 115° = 230°.

mistakes.B: Step 2: 230° is the REFLEX angle AOC (on the same arc as ∠ABC). The non-reflex angle is 360° minus it.
mistakes.C: Step 1: the angle at the centre is double, not half: 2 × 115°.
mistakes.D: Step 1: 180° − 115° gives an angle at the circumference on the other arc. The angle at the centre on that arc is double it.

questions.diagram_alt: A circle with centre O. A and C are on the lower left and lower right, and B is on the circle between them at the bottom. Angle ABC is 115°. Radii OA and OC are drawn and the angle AOC facing B is marked x.

questions.prompt: Two parallel chords are 16 cm and 12 cm long, on opposite sides of the centre of a circle of radius 10 cm. How far apart are the chords?
questions.explanation: The 16 cm chord is √(10² − 8²) = 6 cm from O and the 12 cm chord is √(10² − 6²) = 8 cm from O. On opposite sides, they are 6 + 8 = 14 cm apart. 2 cm would be correct only if they were on the same side.
steps: 16 cm chord: half = 8, distance = √(10² − 8²) = √36 = 6 cm.
12 cm chord: half = 6, distance = √(10² − 6²) = √64 = 8 cm.
Opposite sides of O, so the gap is 6 + 8 = 14 cm.

mistakes.A: Step 3: the chords are on opposite sides of O, so add the distances 6 + 8, don't subtract.
mistakes.B: Step 1: subtracting the chord lengths doesn't give a distance. Find each chord's distance from O with Pythagoras.
mistakes.D: Step 1: 20 cm is the diameter. The chords are not at the top and bottom of the circle; find each distance from O.

questions.diagram_alt: A circle with centre O and radius 10 cm. Two parallel chords: AB, 16 cm long, above O, and CD, 12 cm long, below O. A dashed line through O meets both chords at right angles.

questions.prompt: Which reason best explains why an angle in a semicircle is always 90°?

options.A: The angle at the centre on the diameter is a straight angle, 180°, and the angle at the circumference is half of it
options.B: The triangle formed is equilateral, so each angle is 60° plus 30°
options.C: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add to 180°
options.D: Angles in the same segment are equal, so they are all 90°

questions.explanation: A diameter makes a straight angle of 180° at the centre, and the angle at the circumference on the same arc is half of that: 90°. "Same segment" only shows the angles are equal, not that they are 90°.
steps: The diameter AB passes through O, so ∠AOB is a straight angle: 180°.
Angle at the circumference = half the angle at the centre on the same arc.
So ∠ACB = 180° ÷ 2 = 90° for every C on the circle.

mistakes.B: Step 1: the triangle is not equilateral in general — C can be anywhere on the circle.
mistakes.C: Step 1: a triangle in a semicircle is not a quadrilateral. Use the angle at the centre rule.
mistakes.D: Step 2: equal angles alone don't say what size they are. You still need the centre angle (180°) to get 90°.
